1.title: Architectures and Patterns
1.text: Welcome to Module two: Architectures and Patterns. This module covers architectures and patterns. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. The parts of an end-to-end architecture: input, processing, output and feedback loops. The augmented L L M (large language model) building block. The five workflow patterns and when each fits. Agents: when they are justified, and their costs. How to select a pattern from the problem's shape.

1.title: Case Check-In: Lumen Advisory Designs a Claims Intake for a Health Insurer
1.text: Our running case is Lumen Advisory. Lumen Advisory Designs a Claims Intake for a Health Insurer. Claims arrive as emails, P D F s and portal forms. The system must classify, extract fields, check coverage rules, draft a decision note and let a nurse reviewer approve. Every correction by the reviewer should improve the system.

1.title: An End-to-End Architecture
1.text: An End-to-End Architecture. The figure shows this: An end-to-end architecture: input and ingestion, processing with Claude and tools, output validation, review and action, then feedback and monitoring that loops back.

1.title: An End-to-End Architecture, continued
1.text: An End-to-End Architecture, continued. Input. Responsibilities: Receive, authenticate, normalize, redact, route. Claim-intake example: Parse P D F s, mask personal identifiers, tag the claim type. Processing. Responsibilities: Prompts, retrieval, tools, orchestration, model calls. Claim-intake example: Classify, extract, retrieve coverage rules, draft a note. Output. Responsibilities: Validate shape and content, apply guardrails. Claim-intake example: Schema check, rule check, confidence flag. Action and review. Responsibilities: Human approval, system updates, notifications. Claim-intake example: Nurse approves; claim system updated. Feedback. Responsibilities: Logs, corrections, metrics, evals, drift alerts. Claim-intake example: Reviewer edits become eval cases; accuracy dashboard. Feedback loops are part of the design, not an afterthought: they feed evaluation sets, prompt changes and monitoring (Modules eleven and twelve).

1.title: An End-to-End Architecture, continued
1.text: An End-to-End Architecture, continued. Design for failure paths: retries, fallbacks, escalation to a human, dead-letter queue for bad inputs. Keep deterministic code for checks that must always hold (validation, authorization, totals); use the model for language and judgment. Separate concerns: ingestion, orchestration, model access, tools, storage, observability. This supports testing and replacement. Exam tip: An architecture answer should include validation of model output and a feedback path, not only the model call.

1.title: The Augmented LLM
1.text: The Augmented L L M. The augmented L L M is the basic building block: a model enhanced with retrieval, tools and memory. It can generate its own search queries, choose tools and decide what to retain.

1.title: The Augmented LLM, continued
1.text: The Augmented L L M, continued. The figure shows this: The augmented L L M: a model with retrieval for knowledge, tools for actions and memory for state. Tailor the augmentations to the use case and give the model a well-documented interface (tool names, descriptions, schemas). Most solutions are an augmented L L M inside a workflow: the code controls the path, the model does the language and judgment steps.

1.title: The Augmented LLM, continued
1.text: The Augmented L L M, continued. Integration standards such as M C P (Model Context Protocol) connect tools and data in a reusable way (Module eight).

1.title: Workflow Patterns
1.text: Workflow Patterns. A workflow orchestrates L L M s and tools through predefined code paths.

1.title: Workflow Patterns, continued
1.text: Workflow Patterns, continued. Prompt chaining. How it works: Sequential calls; each uses the previous output; optional gates. Use when: Task splits cleanly into fixed subtasks. Trade-off: More latency, higher accuracy. Routing. How it works: Classify the input, send to a specialized path or model. Use when: Distinct categories; accurate classification; easy versus hard queries. Trade-off: Misrouting risk; classifier needed. Parallelization: sectioning. How it works: Independent subtasks run at once. Use when: Speed; independent aspects. Trade-off: Merge logic. Parallelization: voting. How it works: Same task run several times. Use when: Higher confidence; guardrail checks. Trade-off: Cost multiplies. Orchestrator-workers. How it works: A central model splits work it cannot predict, delegates, synthesizes. Use when: Subtasks depend on the input (multi-file changes, research). Trade-off: Cost, coordination.

1.title: Workflow Patterns, continued
1.text: Workflow Patterns, continued. Evaluator-optimizer. How it works: One model generates, another critiques, loop. Use when: Clear criteria and measurable improvement from feedback. Trade-off: Extra calls; stop rule needed.

1.title: Workflow Patterns, continued
1.text: Workflow Patterns, continued. The figure shows this: Five workflow patterns: prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers and evaluator-optimizer. Chaining trades latency for accuracy; routing can send easy queries to a smaller, cheaper model. Sectioning and voting are the two forms of parallelization; voting gives diversity for confidence checks. Use orchestrator-workers only when the subtasks cannot be listed in advance; otherwise plain parallelization is simpler.

1.title: Workflow Patterns, continued
1.text: Workflow Patterns, continued. Evaluator-optimizer needs clear criteria and a maximum number of rounds.

1.title: Agents
1.text: Agents. An agent is an L L M that dynamically directs its own process and tool use, checks the environment at each step (ground truth) and decides when it is done. The path cannot be predicted or hardcoded. The steps are known. The task is open-ended (research, coding across files). Latency and cost must be low and predictable. You can trust the model's decisions in a sandbox with guardrails. Errors would be costly and hard to undo without gates. Costs: higher token use and latency, and compounding errors across steps.

1.title: Agents, continued
1.text: Agents, continued. Controls: stopping conditions (maximum steps), human checkpoints, sandboxes, tool permissions, tracing. Frameworks (the Claude Agent S D K (software development kit) and others) speed up work but add abstraction that hides prompts and complicates debugging. Start with direct A P I (application programming interface) calls, understand the framework's code, and reduce abstraction for production.

1.title: Selecting a Pattern
1.text: Selecting a Pattern. The figure shows this: Choosing a pattern from the shape of the problem: a single call, a workflow, orchestrator-workers or an agent.

1.title: Selecting a Pattern, continued
1.text: Selecting a Pattern, continued. One step; good context and examples are enough. Single optimized call. Fixed sequence. Prompt chaining. Distinct input types. Routing. Independent parts; speed. Sectioning. Need confidence from diversity. Voting. Unpredictable subtasks. Orchestrator-workers. Quality improves with critique. Evaluator-optimizer. Open-ended path, many tools. Agent. Exam tip: "Steps known in advance" means a workflow; "path depends on what is discovered" means an agent. When both could work, pick the simpler. Exam tip: Validation and a feedback path are part of every end-to-end design; a bare model call is not an architecture.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Stages: Input, processing, output validation, review and action, feedback. Augmented L L M: Model plus retrieval, tools, memory. Workflows: Chaining, routing, sectioning, voting, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer. Agent: Model directs its own path; costs and compounding errors; needs limits and gates. Choose: Known steps equals workflow; unpredictable equals orchestrator-workers or agent; simplest that works. Frameworks: Start with direct A P I calls; reduce abstraction for production. Keep in code: Validation, authorization, exact calculation.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A claims pipeline has five fixed steps, each of which can be validated. Which design is most appropriate? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Known, checkable steps suit a workflow; it is predictable and debuggable.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A support system receives billing, technical and legal questions that need different prompts and tools. Which pattern fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Distinct categories with accurate classification are the routing use case.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. An architect wants higher confidence in a content-safety decision. Which approach does that most directly? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Voting runs the check several times or with several prompts and aggregates the diverse outputs, which raises confidence in the decision.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A coding task requires editing an unknown number of files depending on the request. Which pattern is most suitable? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Unpredictable subtasks that depend on the input are the orchestrator-workers case.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. What is the main risk of choosing an agent for a fixed, well-understood task? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Agents add cost and risk; they pay off only when the path is genuinely unpredictable.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Select two. Which two belong in every end-to-end Claude architecture? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and B. Validation and feedback are core; autonomy without limits and shared credentials are risks.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. A team adopts an agent framework and cannot understand why prompts behave strangely in production. What does this illustrate? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Start simple, understand what the framework does, and reduce abstraction when moving to production.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. In an evaluator-optimizer loop, which design element prevents endless refinement? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Criteria define "good enough" and a round limit bounds cost.

1.title: Practice Question 9
1.text: Question nine. A reviewer's corrections on drafted claim notes are not being captured. Which architectural gap is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Feedback loops convert reviewer work into eval cases and improvements.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all nine answers. Question one: B. Question two: A. Question three: C. Question four: C. Question five: C. Question six: A and B. Question seven: D. Question eight: C. Question nine: A. In the next module, we continue the course.
